claim: LLMs, when verbalizing confidence in a black-box (zero-shot prompted) setting, tend to be overconfident, mimicking human overconfidence patterns.
stance_target: the general finding that untrained/prompted verbalized confidence is unreliable
scope_conditions: 5 dataset types (commonsense/arithmetic reasoning etc.), 5 LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat, general QA/reasoning domain
quoted_support: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence.

claim: White-box methods (using internal model information) only narrowly beat black-box verbalized/consistency methods at failure prediction -- AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 -- indicating the internal-vs-expressed gap in general QA settings, prior to purpose-built probes, was measured as small.
stance_target: the assumption that internal signals dramatically outperform verbalized confidence in all settings
scope_conditions: 5 LLMs, 5 dataset types, general QA, whole-answer granularity, off-the-shelf white-box signals not purpose-trained linear probes
quoted_support: Comparisons with white-box methods indicate that while white-box methods perform better, the gap is narrow, e.g., 0.522 to 0.605 in AUROC.

claim: All confidence-elicitation methods tested (verbalized, consistency-based, white-box) struggle on tasks requiring professional/specialized knowledge, a caveat directly relevant to code as a professional-knowledge domain.
stance_target: generalizability of confidence-elicitation methods to specialized domains like code
scope_conditions: Professional-knowledge-requiring QA subsets within the 5-dataset benchmark
quoted_support: All investigated methods struggle in challenging tasks, such as those requiring professional knowledge, indicating significant scope for improvement.
